implementation_notes: Scala's collections framework is the pattern at the heart of the library: every collection offers map, filter, flatMap, collect, foldLeft/fold, reduce, groupBy and friends, and the documentation states that 'Scala collections are by default strict in all their transformers, except for LazyList' - each transformer builds a complete new collection of the same kind, which is what makes the default form predictable and easy to inspect. for-comprehensions desugar to map/flatMap/withFilter calls, so the pipeline and comprehension forms are the same computation. fold/reduce/sum act as terminals.
code_sketch:
val emails = people
  .filter(_.active)
  .map(_.email)
  .distinct
  .sorted
  .take(10)                       // strict: one collection per stage

val total = orders.foldLeft(0)(_ + _.amount)          // terminal
val byRegion = orders.groupBy(_.region).view.mapValues(_.size).toMap
pitfalls: All transformers are strict: a long chain over a large collection allocates a new collection per stage, and the element type (Vector stays Vector) is re-created each time.
Type inference needs help at chain boundaries (fold over a wider accumulator type, groupBy over mixed subtypes); explicit annotations keep the intermediate types honest.
view.mapValues on the Map returns a view, so the result must be forced with toMap before it is shared or mutated further.

variants.name: Lazy views and LazyList
variants.implementation_notes: Switching a collection to a view (xs.view) or using LazyList makes the transformers non-strict: the documentation defines a view as 'a special kind of collection that represents some base collection, but implements all transformers lazily', with transformers in O(1) and element access traversing as few elements as possible - so a filter/map/take chain builds no intermediate structures and stops as soon as the consumer has enough (the docs' palindrome example). to(...)/force/toList is the terminal that materialises. Prefer it for long chains, large or infinite sources and early termination; the same page warns the closure overhead can outweigh the savings on small collections and that lazy evaluation plus side effects is confusing.
variants.code_sketch:
val palindrome = words.view
  .map(_.toLowerCase)
  .filter(w => w == w.reverse)
  .headOption                     // forces only up to the first match

val fibs = LazyList.iterate((0, 1)) { case (a, b) => (b, a + b) }.map(_._1)
fibs.filter(_ % 2 == 0).take(5).toList
pitfalls: A view is not a collection: printing it shows an unevaluated view, and every traversal re-runs the transformers (and any side effects they contain).
Some operations are always forcing (sorted is called out in the docs), and LazyList's ++ is strict in its argument, so laziness leaks away exactly where it matters.
